name: Esther Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in a medical supplies warehouse that stocks pharmacies and a few clinics. I pick bandages, syringes, test kits and medicines, and every item has a batch number and an expiry date I have to check. It's careful work, not fast work, and I like that. I've been there seven years and I know which shelf has the stuff with the short dates.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal shift look like from start to finish?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at eight, pick until lunch, then do a couple of hours in the cold room where the vaccines are kept, which is two to eight degrees. I finish at half four and drive home. Tomas, my partner, drives a city bus, so we eat late most nights, and I like a quiet evening after a day of counting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never believed most of it anyway. At work I'd say we're still needed because someone has to check the dates properly. I'm not online much, maybe I'd say something in the family group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays where it is, and that's what I want. We have a small flat with a mortgage, about eight months of savings, and both of us have steady jobs. I don't need anything to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just keep going to work and keep paying a bit extra off the mortgage, about 200 a month. Maybe we'd finally book the trip to the lakes that we keep putting off. I wouldn't change anything at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved. Like when the weather forecast says storm and it just rains a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still worry you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My back, a little. The cold room and the lifting add up. And the company has been talking about moving us to a bigger site an hour away, which would mean a longer drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the site moved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably stay, because there are other warehouses nearer home and I'd look there before I'd drive an hour each way. But I'd hate starting somewhere new. I took ages to learn where everything is.

say: She **never believed** most of the AI talk anyway.
Someone still has to **check the dates** properly, so warehouse workers are still needed.
think: Her life **stays where it is**, which is exactly what she wants.
A small flat, **eight months saved** and two steady jobs mean she needs nothing to change.
do: Keep going to work with **no changes** to how she does the job.
Pay about **200 a month** extra off the mortgage.
Finally book the **trip to the lakes** they keep postponing.
feel: **Calm** and relieved, like a storm forecast that brings only rain.
S0.quote: Someone still has to check the expiry dates properly in a medical warehouse. A wrong date on a vaccine isn't a small mistake.
fieldNote: She values **careful work** over speed and is proud of checking batches and dates.
The only real worry is a **site move** an hour away, not AI.
Strongly prefers the **familiar**; starting somewhere new would cost her more than money.

steps.text: Keep checking batches and dates in the cold room as usual
Pay about 200 a month extra off the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds like something for the office people, not for us on the floor. At home I'd say we'll see. I wouldn't post anything, I don't really do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me more for Tomas than for me. Robots spread slowly into hands-on work, so I've got time. But I've read about buses that drive themselves, and the scheduling and ticket office will be AI before that anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and not try any of the AI things. I'd put more into savings, maybe 300 a month instead of extra on the mortgage, so we've got cash if something happens. And I'd ask my manager quietly if the company has any plans for robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's in the background, like a noise in the car you can't find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you switch from the mortgage to savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because cash you can touch. If Tomas had a bad year, the bank won't give us back the extra we paid. My mum taught me that, she lost a job when I was ten and the savings jar saved us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try an AI tool, even to see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I don't see what for. My niece showed me one on her phone and it wrote her a birthday poem for me. It was a nice poem, but she didn't write it, so what's the point.

say: It sounds like a change for the **office people**, not the warehouse floor.
At home she'd just say **we'll see**, and she wouldn't post anything.
think: She has time, because **robots spread slowly** into hands-on work.
She worries more for **Tomas**, her partner, whose bus job could change.
do: Switch **300 a month** from mortgage overpayments into **cash savings**.
Ask her manager **quietly** whether the company plans robots.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a car noise she can't find.
S1.quote: Cash you can touch. When my mum lost her job, the savings jar saved us, and the bank won't give back what we overpaid.
fieldNote: Her worry shifts to her **partner's bus job** more than her own.
A childhood memory of her **mum's job loss** drives her preference for cash.
Firm **refusal of AI tools**; sees no point in them.

steps.text: Move 300 a month from mortgage overpayments into cash savings
Ask her manager quietly about robot plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and the government should slow it down. At work I'd say what everyone would be saying, that nobody knows what's happening. I'd keep my head down mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think we'd both lose our jobs within about three years of each other. The thinking side goes in 2028, so the people who plan routes and the bus timetables and our pick lists are software, and then the robots and self-driving buses come around 2031. We've got a mortgage and eight months of savings, and that's not long for two people out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop the trip, stop any extra spending and put every spare bit into cash. I'd talk to the bank about whether we could fix the mortgage longer. I don't know what job I'd train for, honestly, because I don't know which ones are left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake. I like knowing what tomorrow looks like, and this takes that away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would worry you first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage, 850 a month. Everything else we can cut, the car, the phone plans, the takeaway on Fridays. But if the mortgage goes, we lose the flat, and that flat took us four years to save for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't know what to train for. Would you ask anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably my brother, he's a plumber and seems fine with all this. Maybe I'd go with him for a few weeks to see. But I'm not good at new things, and starting from nothing at thirty scares me.

say: It's **too fast**, and the government should **slow it down**.
At work she'd keep her **head down**, since nobody knows what's happening.
think: She and Tomas could **both lose jobs** within about three years of each other.
**Eight months saved** is not long for two people out of work with a **mortgage**.
do: Cancel the **trip** and stop extra spending at once.
Ask the bank about **fixing the mortgage** for longer.
Talk to her **plumber brother** about trying his trade.
feel: **Alarmed** and lying awake, because she loses knowing **what tomorrow looks like**.
S2.quote: The flat took Tomas (her partner) and me four years to save for, and the mortgage of 850 a month is the bill I'd lie awake over.
fieldNote: A **double household hit**: her picking and her partner's bus driving both end within a few years.
The **850 mortgage** is the bill that frightens her most.
She has **no idea** what to retrain for and admits she's bad at new things.

steps.text: Cancel the lakes trip and stop all extra spending
Ask the bank about fixing the mortgage for longer
Spend a few weeks with her plumber brother on jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, at least. At work I'd say let's see what the company says. I'd want the government to tell us properly what's coming instead of guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it gives us until about 2034 for the hands-on jobs, so I'd be thirty-five. That's still young. But Tomas and I would both have to change, and neither of us likes change much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd build our savings from eight months to a year and stop overpaying the mortgage. I'd watch what happens at work and maybe take the forklift licence the company offers, because it's free and it's still warehouse work. I wouldn't jump to anything else yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not as bad as the fast one. It's like knowing there's an exam coming but not knowing the subject.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a forklift licence help if robots come in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not for long, no. But it's something I can do without leaving where I know. I'd rather do a small step I can manage than a big one I'd fail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tomas say to each other about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas would say he'll drive till they take the keys off him. I'd say we need a plan. We'd end up agreeing to save and not argue about it, which is how we handle most things.

say: The government should explain **what's coming** properly instead of everyone guessing.
think: The hands-on jobs last until about **2034**, when she'd be thirty-five.
Both she and Tomas would have to **change**, and neither likes change.
do: Raise savings from eight months to **a year**, pausing mortgage overpayments.
Take the **free forklift licence** the company offers.
Hold off on any **bigger move** for now.
feel: **Anxious**, like an exam coming with an **unknown subject**.
S3.quote: I'd rather do a small step I can manage than a big one I'd fail, like a forklift licence instead of a whole new trade.
fieldNote: Her plan is **small steps** that keep her in familiar territory.
Admits a forklift licence buys **little time**, but it feels manageable.
The couple **saves rather than argues**, which is how they handle most things.

steps.text: Build savings from eight months to a full year
Take the company's free forklift licence course
Wait to see what the company announces before bigger moves

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can change. At work I'd say the same, let's not panic. I'd want politicians to use the time to make sure nobody falls through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still the same ending, just later. I'd be forty when robots can do my job, and Tomas would be forty-three. Forty is a strange age to start again, but at least we'd have paid more of the mortgage off by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go back to overpaying the mortgage hard, maybe 400 a month, so it's much smaller by 2039. I'd do the forklift licence and later maybe something in pharmacy, like a dispensing assistant course, since I already know medicines. But I'd only start that in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still, but slow. It's there every time I read the news, then I forget it for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why go back to overpaying the mortgage here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years is enough time to make the mortgage small. If it's nearly paid off when the robots come, we could live on one smaller wage. That feels safer to me than a pile in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a dispensing assistant job be safe from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. The checking might be done by a computer by then. But people go to the pharmacy and want to ask a person, especially old people, so maybe. It's the only thing I can think of that uses what I know.

say: **Ten years** is a long time, so nobody should **panic** yet.
Politicians should use the decade to make sure **nobody falls through**.
think: It's the **same ending**, later: she'd be forty and Tomas forty-three.
Paying down **more of the mortgage** by then would make it easier.
do: Overpay the mortgage by about **400 a month** to shrink it by 2039.
Start a **dispensing assistant** course in a few years.
feel: **Anxious** but slow, remembered with each news story and forgotten for a week.
S4.quote: If the mortgage is nearly paid off when the robots come, Tomas (her partner) and I could live on one smaller wage.
fieldNote: With ten years she switches back to **paying down the mortgage**, her idea of safety.
Looks to **pharmacy work** because it builds on her knowledge of medicines.
Honest that she **doesn't know** whether that work will be safe.

steps.text: Overpay the mortgage by about 400 a month
Take a dispensing assistant course in a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits both of us and we'd have no time. What would help is the bank and the government giving people a break on mortgages while they retrain, so you don't lose your home just because the robots came early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples. Everyone talks about one person's job, but Tomas and I share everything. If both our jobs go at the same time, it's not twice as bad, it's worse than that.

headlineQuote: If both our jobs go at the same time, it's not twice as bad, it's worse than that.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old picker** at a medical supplies warehouse who checks every **batch and expiry date**.
She shares a mortgaged flat with Tomas, a **bus driver**, and has about eight months saved.
She prefers the **familiar**, never uses AI, and plans in **small steps**.
Her fear grows with speed: calm when nothing changes, **alarmed at 2028** because both incomes go.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her job and her partner's bus job would go with **no time**.
whatWouldHelp: **Mortgage breaks** from banks and government while people retrain, so families keep their homes.
